entries.title: Kvaratskhelia, Dembele and Marquinhos out injured after PSG’s win
entries.summary: Kvaratskhelia out for months with a torn ACL in his right knee, while Dembele and Marquinhos suffer thigh muscle tears.
entries.content:
Kvaratskhelia out for months with a torn ACL in his right knee, while Dembele and Marquinhos suffer thigh muscle tears.

Paris Saint-Germain have been handed a triple injury setback after their stunning Champions League win over Barcelona, with star players Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Ousmane Dembele and Marquinhos forced out of action in the coming weeks.

Kvaratskhelia sustained an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear in his right knee, making him unavailable for months, while forward Dembele and captain Marquinhos sustained thigh muscle injuries during the match on Tuesday.

“Having suffered a torn anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee during yesterday’s match against FC Barcelona, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia is set to undergo surgery in the coming days,” PSG said in a statement.

Kvaratskhelia landed awkwardly after sprinting back to make a tackle on Xavi Espart early in the second half and looked in severe pain as he clutched his knee.

Last year’s Ballon d’Or winner Dembele (left thigh) and Marquinhos (right thigh) are both set to miss several weeks.

Dembele pulled up clutching the back of his left thigh following a run down the left in the 19th minute of the game.

Kvaratskhelia and 32-year-old Marquinhos were replaced on the hour mark at the Parc des Princes, where two-time defending champions PSG won 4-2 for a third straight win in the competition.

PSG coach Luis Enrique used Dembele sparingly in the French league last season and has already rested him twice in Ligue 1 this campaign.

The France star, who scored six goals at the World Cup, struggled with injuries last season and had been beset by leg muscle injuries at his previous club Barcelona.

The 2024-25 campaign, which led to him winning the men’s Ballon d’Or, saw Dembele playing 50 games overall in a season for the first time in his career.

Kvaratskhelia injured his right ankle last season.

PSG host Lyon in Ligue 1 on Sunday, with both sides level on points at the top of the standings.

entries.title: Why are French protesters chanting ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’?
entries.summary: The slogan has come to represent a whole array of grievances that lie at the heart of the protest movement.
entries.content:
For students, the slogan has come to represent a whole array of grievances that lie at the heart of the protest movement.

As violent protests roil France, bringing together students demanding better educational conditions and groups rejecting the high cost of living, one chant has become an improbable rallying cry: “Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres”.

The unofficial slogan does not mean much taken literally, but students have channelled a whole array of grievances that lie at the heart of the protest movement into this nonsensical expression. It is meant to mock racial stereotyping by the police.

Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets nationwide over the weekend, in the largest mobilisation since protests over education reforms and rising prices began last month. The protest movement has been triggered by grievances ranging from overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages to systemic inequality and lack of opportunity.

Police conduct has also come under scrutiny. France’s police inspectorate, the IGPN, has opened dozens of investigations into alleged police violence since protests began.

What does the slogan mean?

“Bismillah” is Arabic for “in the name of God”, an expression used by Muslims before beginning an activity. In French slang, it has lost some of its original meaning, becoming more akin to “let’s do it”.

“C’est les ténèbres” literally translates as “it’s the darkness”, which alludes to a situation that is bleak and hopeless.

The slogan therefore translates as “In the name of God, it’s the darkness”, which does not convey a clear message in and of itself.

Where did the slogan come from?

Students say the phrase is a mockery of the police force, which tried to infiltrate social media chats used by protesters to coordinate.

The screenshot of a Snapchat conversation featuring the expression began circulating in early October. In it, a user named Mamadou requests to be added to a group, saying: “Hi, in the name of God, it’s the darkness. When’s the blockade, wallah, bro?”

The message also featured emojis with Algerian flags.

Students say the message was sent by undercover police officers attempting to infiltrate their chats by using an unconvincing mix of Arabic and slang. The claim has not been verified and French authorities have not issued any statement.

Youssef El Chazli, associate professor in Arab and Mediterranean sociology at Paris 8 University Vincennes – Saint-Denis, said the phrase “reinforces an image of out-of-touch policemen filled with stereotypes”.

“Such stereotypes appear to disproportionately aim at youths from Arab and African descent,” El Chazli told Al Jazeera. “This appears as one more example of how out-of-touch state agencies seem to be with the current movement.”

What does the slogan tell us about the protest movement?

The slogan has appeared on cardboard placards as a mockery of racial stereotypes and as a symbol of how authorities are out of touch with the realities of young people.

The slogan has spread as far as Italy and Belgium, where similar protests over the high cost of living and poor education also took place over the weekend.

El Chazli said satirical memes and internet trends have become tools to express political grievances during protests, which have traditionally been “inventive and creative”. “With youth mobilisations, protest creativity will draw heavily on youths’ subcultures,” he said.

Discussions around Islamophobia have also taken a front seat in public debate. French authorities have been reluctant to comment publicly on a significant spike in Islamophobic acts in France. One report cited by the Reuters news agency last year showed a 72 percent increase in such incidents during the January-March quarter of 2025 compared with the same period in 2024.

The French far right quickly resorted to racist language to blame Muslim youths for the violence, while United States President Donald Trump also chimed in, claiming that this is about “Islam wanting to take over”.

“What used to be a nonsubject 20 years ago is now a debated point,” El Chazli said. “For younger generations, Arab and African influences have been steadily mainstreaming in youth subcultures, owing to sports and arts figures, as well as new radio shows or social media content.”

entries.title: UK approves development of Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
entries.summary: The decision has drawn sharp criticism from left-wing politicians and environmentalists.
entries.content:
The decision has drawn sharp criticism from left-wing politicians and environmentalists.

The United Kingdom’s government has approved a natural gas project off the coast of Scotland, as the Labour government seeks to balance its climate goals with energy security concerns.

Energy Minister Miatta Fahnbulleh said on Wednesday that the Jackdaw gasfield would begin supplying energy to UK homes by the end of the month and would help to boost the country’s energy security.

The government said the North Sea project would increase UK gas production by about 6 percent at its peak.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the decision will “protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm”, but stressed it would not hinder the government’s targets on renewable energy.

The government also announced a New Energy Wealth Fund, which will invest in renewable and low-carbon energy projects as part of the green transition.

The fund has been established with an initial 2 billion pounds ($2.7bn), with plans to raise additional funds through tax revenues from North Sea oil and gas.

Higher energy prices amid the Russia-Ukraine war and the United States-Israel war on Iran have weighed on households and businesses, dragging on Britain’s economy.

Fahnbulleh told UK radio station LBC that the development of Jackdaw would not bring down household energy bills.

“I think it’s really important that we’re honest about this,” Fahnbulleh said.

“That was not a consideration in the decision because it won’t mean cheaper bills. This was about energy security.”

The announcement has drawn criticism from left-wing politicians and environmental groups.

Zack Polanski, the leader of the opposition Green Party, described the decision as “climate vandalism”.

“Surreal to hear [the] energy secretary try and say this is a ‘pragmatic decision’,” Polanski wrote in a post on X.

“It will do nothing to lower bills. It will do lots for the profits of the oil and gas companies. And will continue us further down the path of floods and wildfires.”

Environmental group Greenpeace said the decision showed “the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy”.

“True pragmatism means severing our reliance on expensive oil and gas that leaves British households broke, supercharges extreme weather, and leaves our energy security at the mercy of petrostates,” said Ami McCarthy, head of politics at Greenpeace UK.

entries.title: WW1 to Houthis: British jets for Saudi Arabia build on long military bond
entries.summary: UK's deployment of jets to defend Saudi Arabia is the latest chapter in a relationship older than the kingdom itself.
entries.content:
The UK’s deployment of jets to defend Saudi Arabia is the latest chapter in a military relationship older than the kingdom itself.

The United Kingdom has announced it will deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to help defend Saudi Arabia from missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, the armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).

The jets will play a “defensive role”, the British Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement on Tuesday, adding that they will not carry out attacks against the Iranian-backed armed group.

The move comes amid heavy fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have carried out missile and drone attacks against the kingdom, including oil facilities and Riyadh’s main airport, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government has launched air attacks on Houthi positions.

The UK’s decision to send jets to assist Saudi Arabia marks just the latest chapter in a partnership that stretches back more than a century, to a treaty signed during the First World War, years before the Saudi kingdom was founded.

So what is the UK sending, and how did the two countries become so closely bound?

Here’s what you need to know:

What is the UK sending?

Fighter jets, an A400M transport aircraft and advisers.

The ministry said it was also extending air-to-air refuelling, which it previously agreed to provide for Saudi air operations, including those to degrade Houthi military targets in Yemen.

How far back does the UK-Saudi relationship go?

To the First World War.

In December 1915, Sir Percy Cox, a senior British official in the Gulf, concluded the Treaty of Darin with King Abdulaziz Ibn Saud, then ruler of Nejd in central Arabia, according to India Office records held by the UK’s National Archives.

In return, he allied with Britain against the Ottoman Empire, and Britain backed him with cash and weapons.

In May 1927, Britain signed a new treaty with him at Jeddah, according to an India Office memorandum.

King Abdulaziz founded the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932.

When did UK-Saudi arms deals begin?

In the 1960s.

In May 1966, Saudi Arabia signed contracts to buy 40 Lightning fighter jets and 25 jet trainers from the British Aircraft Corporation, along with a radar system, according to a US Department of State memo from the time.

Even then, Yemen was part of the picture.

In 1962, the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen was overthrown in a military coup and the Yemen Arab Republic was established. Egypt sent troops to back the republican government, while Saudi Arabia and Jordan armed and funded royalist forces trying to restore the Imam. By 1966, the civil war had reached a stalemate.

Meanwhile, Britain was facing rebellion from Soviet- and Egypt-backed nationalist groups over its control of Aden and southern Yemen. Britain ultimately withdrew in 1967.

In 1966, Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, Prince Sultan, asked the UK to supply an RAF fighter squadron to fly under Saudi colours if fighting resumed in Yemen, according to declassified US State Department records.

Britain instead offered fighter jets flown by British pilots, and said it was ready to send an RAF squadron of Lightning interceptors for a short period if required.

In the end, Saudi Arabia accepted the jets and civilian pilots, and the RAF squadron was not needed, the records show.

BAE Systems, then the British Aircraft Corporation, says its ties with Saudi Arabia date back to 1966, and in 1973, the two governments signed a memorandum of understanding naming the company as prime contractor.

1980s and the Al-Yamamah deal

In 1985, the two governments signed an oil-for-arms agreement, known as Al-Yamamah, for Tornado and Hawk jets.

The Reuters news agency has described the Al-Yamamah deals as the largest export contracts in British history.

Saudi Arabia set aside up to 600,000 barrels of oil a day to pay for Tornado jets and other equipment.

The UK’s Serious Fraud Office investigated corruption allegations linked to the deal from 2004, but dropped the inquiry in December 2006, according to a House of Lords judgement.

The attorney general, Lord Goldsmith, cited the need to safeguard national security.

Has Britain fought from Saudi soil before?

Yes.

When Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, King Fahd of Saudi Arabia asked friendly governments for help.

On August 11, 12 RAF Tornado fighters flew from Akrotiri in Cyprus to Dhahran in Saudi Arabia, according to the RAF Museum.

Further RAF Tornado detachments were set up at Tabuk in Saudi Arabia in October 1990, and at Dhahran in January 1991, the museum’s records show.

During the war, then-Defence Secretary Tom King told Parliament that Saudi Arabia had provided the UK with host-nation support.

He also reported that a Tornado based in the kingdom had gone missing, the fourth lost in enemy action.

British aircraft then patrolled a no-fly zone over southern Iraq, alongside United States and French jets, flying from Saudi bases until 2003, according to the US Air Force.

Where do the Typhoons come in?

In September 2007, Saudi Arabia agreed to buy 72 Typhoons from Britain, the UK MoD said at the time. The jets were to replace Tornadoes and other aircraft in the Saudi air force.

The deal was worth 4.43 billion pounds (then about $8.9bn).

BAE Systems, which builds the jets, called it the Salam Project.

Further RAF Tornado detachments were set up at Tabuk in Saudi Arabia in October 1990 and at Dhahran in January 1991.

In March 2018, during Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to London, the UK signed a memorandum of intent with Saudi Arabia to finalise the purchase of 48 more Typhoons, BAE Systems said in a statement to the London Stock Exchange.

But the deal stalled.

Germany, which helps build the Typhoon and has a veto over its exports, halted arms sales to Saudi Arabia after the killing of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, a columnist for The Washington Post who wrote critically of the crown prince and his policies, in 2018.

Berlin dropped its objection in January 2024, with then-Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock saying the Middle East had become a completely different place since October 7, 2023, when southern Israel was attacked by Hamas and Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza.

BAE said that year it was supporting the UK government in discussions with Saudi Arabia.

What about Yemen?

In June 2019, five years after the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, triggering a brutal civil war, the UK’s Court of Appeal ruled that the government had acted unlawfully by licensing arms sales to Saudi Arabia for possible use in Yemen without assessing whether past incidents had breached international humanitarian law.

New licences were halted. In July 2020, then-Trade Secretary Liz Truss told Parliament they would resume, saying there was not a clear risk the arms would be used in a serious violation of the law.

The UK has also struck the Houthis directly. RAF Typhoons joined US attacks on Yemen in 2024 following Houthi attacks on Israel-linked Red Sea shipping in response to the bombardment of Gaza, according to the MoD.

Then, in September this year, Britain sent a Voyager tanker to assist Saudi Arabia with air-to-air refuelling of fighter jets. The planes it refuels are British-built Typhoons flown by the Saudi air force.

entries.title: Paramilitary hitman linked to British right-wing group Turning Point UK
entries.summary: Al Jazeera exposes UK far right's links to criminal underworld.
entries.content:
Al Jazeera exposes UK far right's links to criminal underworld.

A violent paramilitary linked to a proscribed terror group has close ties to a right-wing student group in the United Kingdom, an Al Jazeera investigation has revealed.

Allan Nesbitt, a convicted criminal who is a member of the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), is linked to Turning Point UK (TPUK).

Our investigation, Contract Killers and the Far Right, began in 2021, when an undercover reporter from Al Jazeera joined TPUK, an independent offshoot of the right-wing US activist group Turning Point USA. TPUK has close ties to several senior British Conservative Party members, as well as to leaders of Reform UK.

TPUK’s CEO Jack Ross stood as a Conservative Party candidate in 2023. Ross introduced Al Jazeera’s undercover reporter to Nesbitt, who is from Glasgow, Scotland.

Ross made clear that he and Nesbitt had a long history together. Ross was filmed by our undercover reporter agreeing to pay Nesbitt thousands of pounds to stage a fake political rally designed to show support for the lifting of UK sanctions against Zimbabwe.

Ross also told Al Jazeera’s undercover operative that for “a certain amount”, Nesbitt and his contacts could arrange physical attacks, saying they could “kick the f*** out of someone. They can start cutting people’s faces up. That’s another amount. They can stab someone,” Ross said. “They can shoot someone. They could kill someone.”

Murder for hire, caught on tape

To test Ross’s claims about Nesbitt, Al Jazeera’s undercover operative devised a story about a business dispute with a fictional rival they wanted “dealt with”.

In a private meeting in a London hotel, Nesbitt told our reporters he could “arrange whatever you need done”, but “at a price”. This included killing the fictional person with the help of his UVF connections.

“He can have a bad accident,” Nesbitt said, confirming to Al Jazeera that the person would be “finished”.

“These c***s are terrorists. They’re f***ing trained killers,” Nesbitt added.

Nesbitt also claimed to have personally killed before.

“Things have happened in the past where it was too risky to do that [gestures firing a gun], and I’ve just pulled out a knife and stabbed the c*** to death,” he said.

In a later video call, Nesbitt showed off a shotgun, a pistol, and live ammunition to prove he had the means to follow through.

Weapons smuggling

The money paid for the murder would be used to arm the UVF in Northern Ireland, Nesbitt said.

“All the money gets raised in Scotland and the things get bought in Scotland and we smuggle them into Ireland.”

According to Nesbitt, he has been involved in this weapons smuggling for many years.

“It’s us that smuggled the stuff into Ireland for them to fight the war in there,” he said, referring to The Troubles.

During that period, which began in the late 1960s, Catholic and Protestant groups in Northern Ireland fought over whether Protestant-majority Northern Ireland should remain part of the UK or join the Catholic-majority Republic of Ireland.

Those in favour of Northern Ireland remaining a part of the UK are widely known as unionists or loyalists. Those seeking to break from the UK usually identify themselves as republicans or Irish nationalists.

The UVF belonged to the Protestant loyalist side and was responsible for some of the most infamous killings and murders during The Troubles, according to Patricia Devlin, a journalist who has been investigating the group for years.

“Between 1966 and 1999, the UVF killed over 500 people,” she told Al Jazeera.

“They went on to commit atrocities such as the 1971 McGurk’s bar bomb massacre, which killed 15 people, and the 1974 Dublin and Monaghan bombings, which killed 33 people”, she added.

But after the 1998 Good Friday Agreement that at least officially ended the Troubles, the UVF, like many other groups, transformed into a more traditional criminal gang.

“The movement has turned into drug gangs, while still using the name of the UVF,” Devlin said.

To Roy McComb, former deputy director of the UK’s National Crime Agency, Nesbitt’s claims are no surprise.

“The history of loyalism between Northern Ireland [and] Scotland is a very strong and very longstanding one.

“Operationally, there’s certainly evidence previously of firearms being trafficked, of intelligence being shared, of activists being moved between the two countries [Scotland and Northern Ireland].

“Firearms … are simply tools that can be sold and that could be sold onto the far right.”

Far-right groups

Besides links to the UVF, Al Jazeera’s investigation also shows links between Turning Point UK and other far-right agitators in the UK. These include groups that have been at the forefront of protests against migrants and LGBTQ+ rights.

“Turning Point UK are fanboys of these kinds of people. These people are obviously a lot more physically tough than Turning Point UK. Turning Point UK know that they put these little, no far right allowed at the bottom just to protect themselves,” Ciaran O’Connor, senior analyst at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, told Al Jazeera.

“They use these events as wedge issues upon which to try and mobilise their support and try and attack the message or the meaning of the other side, and demonise the housing of asylum seekers in society,” he added.

A former member of the UVF told Al Jazeera that the “far right in the UK is a toothless tiger”, but links between the far right and groups like the UVF could change that.

“It changes whenever you make a connection to individuals who are behind a terrorist campaign for probably 40 years, and are still armed, and still have the ability to shoot and bomb,” the former UVF member said.

“Then you’re in trouble.”

Al Jazeera notified Scottish police about Allan Nesbitt and his weapons in the interest of public safety.

Jack Ross denied our findings “completely”, telling us that everything he said to our undercover reporter was not meant seriously.

The other parties featured did not respond to our inquiries.

See the full Al Jazeera investigation here

entries.title: Attack on Australian MP Haines: How threats against legislators have soared
entries.summary: Abuse, threats against Australian lawmakers are rising in a country where political violence has historically been rare.
entries.content:
Abuse and threats against Australian lawmakers are rising in a country where political violence has historically been rare.

An Australian independent lawmaker, Helen Haines, has had both legs amputated after ⁠being struck by a car outside her office in Wangaratta, Victoria state, in what Prime Minister ⁠Anthony Albanese called “a deliberate attack”.

The MP’s right leg was amputated on Wednesday, two days after her left leg was amputated at a hospital in Melbourne, where the 65-year-old politician has been receiving treatment after being flown by helicopter.

“The good news in all this is that Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family,” her husband, Phil Haines, told reporters outside the Melbourne hospital.

“We are grateful and thankful that, at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape,” he said.

The Australian police said it was a “targeted attack” and warned of growing “online extremism” and recorded a rise in abuse, threats and intimidation targeting lawmakers – steadily growing in a country where political violence has been rare.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has led an outpouring of support for Haines. “It’s a reminder that the world is a more dangerous and divided place than it was a generation ago,” Albanese told ABC Radio on Wednesday.

“I think that Australians do want to see their politicians be able to go about their business, to be able to get something from the back of their car, for goodness sake.”

So, why have threats against Australian lawmakers risen?

What do we know about the alleged attack?

On Monday, Haines, who entered parliament in 2019, was struck by an SUV in Wangaratta in the afternoon, sending the rural Australian town into a mix of horror and disbelief.

Haines was getting something from the boot of her car when her alleged attacker drove past in a Toyota Land Cruiser. Authorities said the 43-year-old man turned the car around before veering at Haines and pinning her against her vehicle. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the driver then reversed before ramming her again.

Police named the suspect in the attack as Brendan Nugent, who appeared in court on Wednesday but did not apply for bail or enter a plea.

He was charged with three offences: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a public official. Additional charges of cannabis cultivation and possession have also been laid against him.

Nugent will remain in custody until his next court appearance in February.

The Australian Federal Police received no warning of any imminent danger from the alleged attacker, Commissioner Krissy Barrett told reporters.

“What I can ⁠say is we didn’t have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon,” she said.

Victoria Police Chief Mike Bush said the state police could not find any direct past contact ⁠between Haines and the accused.

“Motivation is one of ⁠these things that we absolutely need to explore. His motivation for this, what we allege is a deliberate attack, is very much a centrepiece of the investigation,” Bush said.

Who is Helen Haines?

Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action. She retained the rural seat of Indi in 2022 and 2025.

She was widely praised for her efforts to increase transparency in politics and crack down on corruption.

“My background in nursing guides my work. As a nurse and a midwife, you’re with people in their most joyous and difficult moments. It’s taught me that life is precious, that everyone deserves dignity and respect, that good policy starts with listening, and – as a health researcher – that facts matter,” she describes herself on her website.

“Every day, I work to be a strong, independent voice – guided by common sense, decency and a commitment to delivering for our community and your family.”

In parliament, she pushed for a national anticorruption body. She introduced a bill in 2021 for a federal integrity commission, but it was defeated.

A year later, the Australian Parliament passed the National Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2022, leading to the formation of the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC).

Haines, who played a major role in the passing of the bill, served as the deputy chair of the parliamentary committee on the NACC.

Why are threats against lawmakers rising?

The Australian Human Rights Commission said the attack happened “against a backdrop of increasing polarisation and threats against politicians” that could undermine democracy.

Threats against Australian lawmakers and electorate offices doubled between 2021 and 2025, with 1,067 incidents reported to police last year.

The police also charged 41 people with offences relating to threats against parliamentarians last year, after the Australian federal police formed a National Security Investigations team described by police commissioner Barrett as a “flying squad of hate disruptors”.

In the 2025 election, threats to candidates jumped 17 percent from the previous campaign.

Earlier this month, police charged three men over separate threats to politicians and government officials, and three others were sentenced by courts.

Senior opposition politician James Paterson on Wednesday called for a review of personal security in response to the alleged crime. “The reality is that Australian parliamentarians by global standards are uniquely accessible to the public and that’s a good thing,” Paterson told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.

“But we can’t have a situation where shocking attacks like this take place because that will fundamentally change our democracy forever if it becomes a serious risk to your life to be a member of parliament,” he added.

Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Director-General Mike Burgess warned last year that politically motivated violence was among the agency’s fastest-growing security concerns, driven by “grievance narratives, conspiracies and online echo chambers”.

Antiterrorism police are among the agencies investigating the attack on Haines, but the police maintain that they believe it was an isolated incident and there was “no intelligence to suggest any threat to Haines”.

What do we know about the attacker?

Nugent, a 43-year-old resident of the rural town of Tarrawingee within Haines’s electorate, has been charged with offences that carry a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.

The motive remains unknown, and authorities have refused to speculate while the investigation takes place.

But police said on Wednesday they were examining all possible leads, including that Nugent may have held radical antigovernment views.

“Like everyone, we’re examining social media associations, talking to witnesses, friends and colleagues,” Bush, the Victoria police commissioner, told journalists.

During the brief court appearance on Wednesday, Nugent’s lawyer said his client suffers from a rare neurological condition called idiopathic transverse myelitis and that it was his first time in custody.

Meanwhile, Wangaratta’s Mayor Irene Grant said a sombre mood has settled over the town of about 30,000 people, a regional hub about 250km (155 miles) northeast of state capital Melbourne.

“What has happened to Helen has caused the community to step back in utter disbelief. We can’t believe it; people are horrified by what has happened,” she told AFP news agency.

entries.title: Blast heard in Yemen’s Aden as Houthis claim attack on military camp
entries.summary: Smoke seen rising near airport in Aden as Houthis say they attacked a military camp with a ballistic missile.
entries.content:
Smoke seen rising near airport in Aden as Houthis say they attacked a military camp with a ballistic missile.

A powerful explosion was heard in Aden in southern Yemen, an Al Jazeera journalist and police have said, as the Houthis claimed a ballistic missile attack on a military camp in the city.

A police official said on Wednesday that smoke was rising near the international airport in Aden, the seat of power of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

Yahya Saree, spokesman of the Houthi armed group, also known as Ansar Allah, meaning Supporters of God in Arabic, said in a statement the attack targeted a military camp used by the Saudi-led coalition, which has been battling the Houthis since a 2022 ceasefire in Yemen’s war collapsed earlier this year.

“Our armed forces were able to target the Saudi enemy’s operations room in the Badr camp in Aden with a ballistic missile,” Saree said in a statement, adding that “the strike was precise and direct”.

There was no immediate comment on the claim from the Yemeni government or the Saudi-led coalition.

The attack was the third on Aden in a week. On Friday, two missiles landed within the perimeter of the city’s airport, with the Houthis claiming the attack.

A day earlier, the group launched a deadly missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden, hitting command centres located inside the compound, which is used by government forces and the Saudi-led coalition.

Elsewhere in Yemen, the Saudi-led coalition said its forces were engaged in heavy fighting with the Houthis in Kahboub in the southwest.

A coalition spokesperson said they were trying to repel a large-scale attack and were experiencing intense Houthi bombardment, describing the situation as “very dangerous”.

Clashes are ongoing under “intensive air cover” by coalition and Yemeni forces, the spokesperson said.

In a separate statement, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted five drones launched towards the kingdom, including in the Medina region, home to one of Islam’s holiest cities.

“Four drones launched towards the kingdom have been intercepted and destroyed,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X, adding in a second post that the interceptions took place in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern province as well as Medina.

Al-Malki, who did not specify who was behind the launches, later said another drone had been intercepted in the Eastern province.

The Houthis denied having targeted the kingdom, with Saree saying their forces had not carried out any “deep” operations in Saudi territory.

Fighting in Yemen escalated sharply last month when the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast.

Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, have been responding with a counteroffensive and have started Operation Dawn of Yemen, which aims to seize and recapture territory from the Houthis, including the capital, Sanaa, which has been under the group’s control since 2014.

entries.title: Australian MP loses both legs in vehicle attack as suspect appears in court
entries.summary: Independent lawmaker Helen Haines is in stable condition, her husband says, as suspect charged with three offences.
entries.content:
Independent lawmaker Helen Haines is in stable condition, her husband says, as suspect charged with three offences.

Australian independent lawmaker Helen Haines has had both of her legs amputated after being rammed by a car outside her electoral office, her husband said, as the suspected attacker appeared in court.

Doctors amputated the MP’s left leg after an attacker hit her twice with his car in Wangaratta, northeast of Melbourne, on Monday, Phil Haines said. They tried to save her right leg but failed to do so, he told a news conference on Wednesday.

“The good news in all this is Helen is alive, and she’s stable,” he told reporters. “That is the most important thing for our family.”

The suspect in the attack, revealed to be a 43-year-old man called Brendan Nugent, made a brief court appearance on Wednesday.

He has been charged with three crimes: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing injury and causing harm to a public official.

He was also charged with the cultivation and possession of cannabis, according to court filings.

The suspect’s lawyer said he has a rare neurological condition called idiopathic transverse myelitis and is also recovering from a concussion, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported.

Police are still investigating the motive for the attack. Australia’s federal police commissioner Krissy Barrett said there was no intelligence suggesting any threat to Haines.

“What I can ⁠say is we didn’t have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon,” she told reporters.

Haines had worked in nursing, midwifery and academia ‌before being elected to parliament in 2019 for the rural seat of Indi, which she retained in 2022 and 2025.

Attacks on politicians are rare in Australia, but concerns have been growing in recent years as online abuse and threats against elected officials have risen.
